title: Donald Trump and Don Jr. tap campaign lawyer Jesse Binnall for Swalwell lawsuit
description_short: Donald Trump and Don Jr. tap campaign lawyer Jesse Binnall for Swalwell lawsuit
description_medium: On March 24, 2021, reports said campaign lawyer Jesse Binnall would represent Donald Trump and Donald Trump Jr. in Representative Eric Swalwell’s civil suit over the January 6 attack. Swalwell accused Trump, his son, Rudy Giuliani and Representative Mo Brooks of conspiring to obstruct Congress’s certification of Joe Biden’s victory and incite violence. The allegations had not been decided by a court.
description_long:
Representative Eric Swalwell filed a civil lawsuit on March 5, 2021, against Donald Trump, Donald Trump Jr., Rudy Giuliani and Representative Mo Brooks. He alleged that they conspired to violate the rights of members of Congress and to delay or prevent certification of Joe Biden’s election victory during the January 6 attack. The complaint also invoked District of Columbia laws concerning inciting a riot and terrorism.

On March 24, reports said Jesse Binnall would represent the Trumps. Binnall had served on Trump’s campaign legal team and had previously worked with Sidney Powell on matters involving Michael Flynn and election-related organizations. His representation was a development in the pending civil case, not a ruling on Swalwell’s allegations. The linked account also said Binnall represented Trump in a separate suit involving Giuliani and members of the Proud Boys and Oath Keepers. The lawsuit’s claims remained allegations at the time of the report; the source excerpt does not describe the defendants’ responses or later court outcome.
organization_tags: U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia

title: Trump: Hungarian and Russian officials caught on intercepts coordinating to block Ukraine from EU
description_short: Trump: Hungarian and Russian officials caught on intercepts coordinating to block Ukraine from EU
description_medium: A report by Michael Weiss and other journalists said an intercepted call captured Hungarian Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó briefing Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov during an EU meeting on Ukraine’s membership talks. Hungary’s Viktor Orbán had threatened to veto opening negotiations, and the report said Lavrov approved the pressure strategy. The account describes reported intercepts, not an EU decision to block Ukraine’s accession.
description_long:
At a December 14, 2023, European Council meeting in Brussels, EU leaders considered opening membership negotiations with Ukraine and Moldova. The linked investigative report said Hungary’s Prime Minister Viktor Orbán threatened to veto the decision while disputing the European Union’s withholding of more than €22 billion in funds over rule-of-law concerns.

The report described an intercepted call in which Hungarian Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó left the meeting to speak with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. In the quoted exchange, Szijjártó explained Hungary’s plan for the meeting, and Lavrov praised the strategy as a form of “direct blackmailing.” The reporting characterized the conversation as evidence of close coordination between Hungarian and Russian officials. It documents what the investigation said the intercept captured; it does not show that Hungary succeeded in preventing Ukraine’s accession negotiations, which EU leaders opened at that meeting. The call’s significance lies in the reported discussion of Hungary’s veto threat with Moscow while an EU decision was underway.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Hungarian and Russian officials caught on intercepts coordinating to block Ukraine from EU
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Hungarian and Russian officials caught on intercepts coordinating to block Ukraine from EU

title: Trump: Senior U.S. Treasury official quits after DOGE attempts to access sensitive payment systems
description_short: Trump: Senior U.S. Treasury official quits after DOGE attempts to access sensitive payment systems
description_medium: Senior Treasury career official David A. Lebryk announced his retirement after a dispute with Elon Musk’s DOGE representatives over access to the department’s payment system. Treasury’s Bureau of the Fiscal Service operates the system, which sends Social Security, Medicare, federal salary and tax-refund payments totaling more than $6 trillion annually. Lebryk had worked at Treasury since 1989 and was serving as acting secretary during the transition.
description_long:
David A. Lebryk, Treasury’s highest-ranking career official, announced his retirement on January 31, 2025, after a dispute with representatives of Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency over access to Treasury payment systems. Lebryk had served at the department since 1989 and was acting secretary until Scott Bessent’s confirmation.

The system at issue, managed by the Bureau of the Fiscal Service, handles more than $6 trillion in federal payments, including Social Security and Medicare benefits, federal salaries and tax refunds. Access had been limited to a small group of career officials because the system controls the movement of sensitive funds. The linked account said DOGE representatives had sought access after the 2024 election and intensified their requests after Trump took office; Treasury staff considered the request unusual and potentially dangerous. Lebryk’s retirement followed the dispute, though the source does not quote him explaining his decision. The event raised questions about who could access payment infrastructure and what safeguards would govern that access.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Senior U.S. Treasury official quits after DOGE attempts to access sensitive payment systems

title: Trump: French researcher is first-known case of denied entry to U.S. of anti-Trump travelers
description_short: Trump: French researcher is first-known case of denied entry to U.S. of anti-Trump travelers
description_medium: A French space researcher was reportedly searched at Houston’s airport after officials found messages criticizing the Trump administration’s science policy on the researcher’s phone. The researcher’s devices were reportedly confiscated and the person was returned to Europe the next day. French higher-education minister Philippe Baptiste condemned the decision, saying the messages expressed a personal opinion. The researcher’s identity and the legal basis for refusing entry were not reported.
description_long:
The linked account reported that a French space researcher was stopped at a Houston airport in March 2025. U.S. officials allegedly searched the person’s work computer and personal phone and found messages criticizing the Trump administration’s treatment of scientists. The researcher was reportedly sent back to Europe the following day, without the devices. The account does not identify the researcher.

Philippe Baptiste, France’s minister for higher education and research, described the person’s messages as exchanges with colleagues and friends expressing a personal opinion about U.S. research policy. Baptiste said he regretted the decision by U.S. authorities. He was commenting on the researcher’s case; he was not the person stopped at the airport. The reports also said the researcher had published an open letter inviting American scientists to move to France. The incident documents a reported device search and denial of entry linked to private messages, but the available account does not give the legal basis for the decision or a U.S. agency explanation.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: French researcher is first-known case of denied entry to U.S. of anti-Trump travelers

title: Trump allies draft executive order to take control over elections
description_short: Trump allies draft executive order to take control over elections
description_medium: Trump allies circulated a draft executive order that would ban mail ballots and voting machines, using claims about foreign interference as a national-security justification. The draft was not signed by Trump. Lawyer Peter Ticktin and activist Cleta Mitchell were among its promoters; Ticktin acknowledged that states, not the president, ordinarily control election administration and argued the alleged foreign threat justified federal action.
description_long:
On April 12, 2025, Trump allies published a draft executive order that proposed federal control over election procedures, including bans on mail-in voting and voting machines. The document invoked foreign interference as a national-security rationale. Its circulation did not make it an executive order: Trump did not sign the draft, and the Constitution assigns states a central role in administering elections.

Florida lawyer Peter Ticktin advocated for the proposal and said the president normally lacked authority over how states conduct elections, but argued that foreign interference could create an emergency. Cleta Mitchell, an election activist and lawyer, was also involved in promoting the draft. The linked account said the activists claimed to be coordinating with the White House, but it did not establish that the administration had adopted the document. The proposal therefore records an effort by Trump allies to expand presidential control over voting; it should not be described as a policy that took effect. The difference between a circulated draft and a signed order is central to its status.

preserved_fields.title: Trump allies draft executive order to take control over elections
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump allies draft executive order to take control over elections

title: Trump orders DOJ investigation of ActBlue, largest Democrat fundraising platform
description_short: Trump orders DOJ investigation of ActBlue, largest Democrat fundraising platform
description_medium: Trump signed a memorandum directing Attorney General Pam Bondi to investigate allegations of straw and foreign donations through online fundraising platforms, amid congressional scrutiny of ActBlue. The memo cited a House report saying ActBlue had identified 22 significant fraud campaigns and 237 donations from foreign IP addresses using prepaid cards. Those figures and allegations did not establish that ActBlue committed fraud; the memo ordered an investigation.
description_long:
On April 24, 2025, Trump signed a memorandum directing Attorney General Pam Bondi, in consultation with the Treasury secretary, to investigate allegations that online fundraising platforms were used for straw or foreign political contributions. The memorandum followed Republican scrutiny of ActBlue, a major fundraising platform for Democratic candidates and organizations.

The memo cited a House investigation that said ActBlue had detected at least 22 significant fraud campaigns, nearly half with a foreign connection, and 237 donations from foreign IP addresses using prepaid cards during a 30-day period in the 2024 campaign. These figures describe activity the platform said it had detected; they are not findings that ActBlue knowingly accepted illegal donations. The directive ordered an investigation and appropriate enforcement if warranted. It did not announce charges or establish that the allegations were true. The linked account also noted that the memo did not mention the Republican fundraising platform WinRed, a detail relevant to questions about the scope of the administration’s scrutiny.

preserved_fields.title: Trump orders DOJ investigation of ActBlue, largest Democrat fundraising platform
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump orders DOJ investigation of ActBlue, largest Democrat fundraising platform

title: Trump: DHS official says more arrests of Democratic lawmakers are coming
description_short: Trump: DHS official says more arrests of Democratic lawmakers are coming
description_medium: On CNN, Homeland Security spokesperson Tricia McLaughlin said more arrests of Democratic lawmakers were “likely” after ICE detained Newark Mayor Ras Baraka outside a detention facility. She claimed the department had body-camera footage of lawmakers assaulting officers and said arrests were under consideration. The linked account disputes McLaughlin’s description that Baraka “stormed” the facility; the statement was not an announcement of charges or completed arrests.
description_long:
On May 10, 2025, Department of Homeland Security spokesperson Tricia McLaughlin told CNN that more arrests were likely after ICE detained Newark Mayor Ras Baraka during a visit to an immigration facility. She said DHS had body-camera footage showing members of Congress assaulting officers and said arrests of lawmakers who were present were “definitely on the table” as part of an ongoing investigation.

McLaughlin also said Baraka had “stormed” the facility. The linked account says footage showed him being taken into custody outside the gate, and that he opposed the facility in his city. Her remarks were a public description of possible future enforcement, not confirmation that additional lawmakers had been arrested or charged. The episode connected a local dispute over an ICE facility with a federal investigation into the conduct of the mayor and visiting lawmakers. The supplied report does not identify the lawmakers or provide the body-camera footage or later charging decisions.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: DHS official says more arrests of Democratic lawmakers are coming
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: DHS official says more arrests of Democratic lawmakers are coming

title: Trump: Pete Hegseth and lawyer lied to White House about leaks
description_short: Trump: Pete Hegseth and lawyer lied to White House about leaks
description_medium: The Guardian reported that White House advisers lost confidence in a Pentagon leak investigation after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s lawyer, Tim Parlatore, said a warrantless wiretap had found a classified document on an aide’s phone. Parlatore later denied saying a wiretap was used and said he had repeated information from Pentagon officials. The inquiry was transferred to Deputy Defense Secretary Stephen Feinberg; the reporting does not establish that either man knowingly lied.
description_long:
The Guardian reported a breakdown in trust between the White House and Pentagon over an investigation into leaks of military information. Tim Parlatore, Hegseth’s personal lawyer and the person overseeing the inquiry, told White House advisers that investigators had used a warrantless wiretap to find classified material on the phone of Dan Caldwell, then a senior Hegseth adviser.

When White House officials questioned how Parlatore knew about the alleged wiretap, he later denied that one had taken place and said Pentagon officials had supplied the information. The reporting said the Air Force Office of Special Investigations had initially focused on mid-level aides and turned to Caldwell and two others around the time they were fired. Caldwell maintained his innocence. The leak investigation was transferred from Parlatore to Deputy Defense Secretary Stephen Feinberg. The linked account documents conflicting descriptions of how the wiretap claim arose and a loss of confidence in the inquiry; it does not establish that Hegseth or Parlatore knowingly made a false statement.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Pete Hegseth and lawyer lied to White House about leaks
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Pete Hegseth and lawyer lied to White House about leaks

title: Trump pulls nomination of NASA head for no clear reason
description_short: Trump pulls nomination of NASA head for no clear reason
description_medium: Trump withdrew Jared Isaacman’s nomination to lead NASA on May 31, 2025, citing a “thorough review of prior associations” without identifying them. The linked report records Laura Loomer’s speculation that Isaacman’s friendship with Elon Musk contributed to the decision, but does not establish that explanation. The specific associations Trump’s review considered and the Senate’s status on the nomination remain unclear.
description_long:
On May 31, 2025, Trump announced that he was withdrawing Jared Isaacman’s nomination to lead NASA. He cited a “thorough review of prior associations” but did not specify which relationships or activities prompted the decision. The linked account notes that Isaacman was a billionaire and CEO of payment-processing company Shift4.

Conservative commentator Laura Loomer suggested that Isaacman’s friendship with Elon Musk could have contributed to the withdrawal, shortly after Musk left the administration. That explanation was speculation, not a reason Trump publicly gave or evidence of what the review found. The source records the withdrawal and the brief rationale; it does not identify the associations at issue or explain whether the Senate had begun acting on the nomination. Those unanswered questions limit what can be said about the motive. The reported event is the removal of a nominee from consideration, not a final decision about Isaacman’s qualifications or NASA’s leadership.

preserved_fields.title: Trump pulls nomination of NASA head for no clear reason
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump pulls nomination of NASA head for no clear reason

notes: Needs context: Trump’s statement cited only a “thorough review of prior associations” and did not identify them. The linked account presents Laura Loomer’s Musk-related explanation as speculation; it supplies no review findings or clear Senate timeline to establish why the nomination was withdrawn.

title: Trump: RFK Jr. fires all CDC vaccine panel members
description_short: Trump: RFK Jr. fires all CDC vaccine panel members
description_medium: On June 9, 2025, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. dismissed all 17 members of the CDC’s vaccine advisory committee, days before its scheduled June 25 meeting. HHS said the meeting would proceed. The dismissal reversed Kennedy’s confirmation-hearing assurance to Senator Bill Cassidy that he would not alter the panel; the linked account says the members were screened for conflicts and that the panel’s recommendations affected vaccine access.
description_long:
On June 9, 2025, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. removed all 17 members of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, the panel that advises the agency on vaccine policy. HHS said the committee’s June 25 meeting would proceed, although replacements had not yet been announced.

The decision conflicted with Kennedy’s assurance to Senator Bill Cassidy during his confirmation hearings that he would not alter the panel. Kennedy later argued that members had pharmaceutical conflicts of interest; the linked account said ACIP members were screened for conflicts and barred from holding vaccine-company stock or serving on manufacturers’ boards. The article also connected the panel’s absence to uncertainty after the CDC changed its COVID-19 vaccine recommendation for pregnant women, with the June meeting expected to address the issue. The dismissal changed who would review vaccine recommendations at a consequential time. It did not itself determine the scientific merits of a vaccine or establish that every former member was free of conflicts.
organization_tags: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services

preserved_fields.title: Trump: RFK Jr. fires all CDC vaccine panel members
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: RFK Jr. fires all CDC vaccine panel members
